terminal_record.title: Robert Maxwell Elected Labour MP for Buckingham in 1964
terminal_record.description_short: Official UK election results list Ian Robert Maxwell as Labour's winning candidate for Buckingham on October 15, 1964.
terminal_record.description_medium: UK Parliament’s 1964 General Election record lists Ian Robert Maxwell as Labour’s winning candidate for Buckingham. Hansard records his Commons service from October 15, 1964, through June 18, 1970. The supplied timeline’s intelligence claims and Trump framing are not established by those historical records; this draft leaves both questions unresolved and is not publication eligible.
terminal_record.description_long: UK Parliament’s 1964 General Election results list Ian Robert Maxwell as the Labour candidate elected for Buckingham, with 23,085 votes. Hansard records his constituency service beginning October 15, 1964, and ending June 18, 1970. These records correct the frozen entry’s October 16 date by one day. The supplied account also claims that Maxwell had KGB and Mossad connections and presents the election under a Trump heading. The historical election sources accessed for this repair establish the constituency, party, result, and parliamentary dates; they do not establish the intelligence claims or explain why Maxwell’s election itself belongs in a Trump-related timeline. The TrumpFile page repeats the election and party information, but its intelligence assertion is not documented in the accessed material. This internal draft retains the bounded election fact, removes unsupported intelligence language, and marks the Trump connection as unresolved. It does not claim that the election was caused by, directed by, or materially connected to Donald Trump. Unless a separate source establishes a meaningful connection to Trump, the entry should not be published in a Trump-focused chronology.
terminal_record.date_basis: Official parliamentary result and Hansard list 1964-10-15; frozen record date 1964-10-16 is corrected. Trump relevance remains unresolved.

terminal_record.title: Kushner's Initial SF-86 Omitted Foreign-Government Contacts
terminal_record.description_short: Kushner's initial SF-86 omitted foreign-government contacts; the 100+ figure was reported later.
terminal_record.description_medium: Jared Kushner’s initial SF-86 was submitted on January 18, 2017, and omitted foreign-government contacts, according to his later statement and his lawyer’s comments to Politico. He said supplemental information followed the next day. The figure of more than 100 contacts was reported in July 2017, so it does not belong to the record’s May 25 date.
terminal_record.description_long: Jared Kushner submitted his initial SF-86 security questionnaire on January 18, 2017. In a July statement to the Senate Judiciary Committee, he said the filing was a rough draft submitted prematurely after his assistant misunderstood a message; the form did not list any foreign-government contacts. He said supplemental information was sent the next day. His explanation is attributed to him and does not independently establish why the form was incomplete. On July 16, Politico quoted Kushner’s attorney Jamie Gorelick saying the original submission omitted all contacts with foreign-government officials and that later materials included more than 100 calls or meetings with representatives of more than 20 countries. That later figure should not be assigned to the May 25 date in the source record: it was reported in July, months after the initial form. This repair dates the event to the January 18 filing and places the 100+ figure in the later supplementation context. The available material establishes the omission and reported correction, but not deliberate concealment, any particular clearance outcome, or the original synopsis’s suggestion that the contacts materially affected the FBI counterintelligence inquiry.

terminal_record.title: P.L. 119-21 Retains Lawful Permanent Residents on SNAP Eligibility List
terminal_record.description_short: The 2025 law’s SNAP eligibility list expressly includes lawful permanent residents.
terminal_record.description_medium: Public Law 119-21, approved July 4, 2025, rewrote SNAP’s noncitizen eligibility subsection. Its list expressly includes lawful permanent residents, so the claim that the law eliminated SNAP eligibility for green-card holders generally is inaccurate. The accessed statutory text does not establish the number affected or verify the supplied note about the existing five-year bar.
terminal_record.description_long: On July 4, 2025, Public Law 119-21 amended section 6(f) of the Food and Nutrition Act of 2008, SNAP’s eligibility provision. The amendment lists who may qualify: U.S. citizens or nationals; lawful permanent residents; people granted Cuban and Haitian entrant status; and people lawfully residing under a Compact of Free Association. It also says an individual must be a U.S. resident and a household must otherwise qualify under section 6. Because lawful permanent residents appear expressly in the enacted list, the claim that the law eliminated SNAP eligibility for green-card holders generally is inaccurate. The text does not establish how many people lost eligibility or the effects on food access, and this card makes no numerical impact claim. The supplied research note says a prior five-year bar continues to apply to some lawful permanent residents, but I did not verify that detail in the text accessed here, so it is excluded from the asserted description. The source resolves the title’s blanket statement; it does not by itself establish every category that lost eligibility compared with prior law.

source_fact_map.fact: The Public Law was approved on July 4, 2025.
Section 10108 addresses alien SNAP eligibility and amends Food and Nutrition Act section 6(f).
source_fact_map.source_excerpt:
SEC. 10108. ALIEN SNAP ELIGIBILITY.

    Section 6(f) of the Food and Nutrition Act of 2008 (7 U.S.C. 
2015(f)) is amended to read as follows:
    ``(f) No individual who is a member of a household otherwise 
eligible to participate in the supplemental nutrition assistance program 
under this section shall be eligible to participate in the supplemental 
nutrition assistance program as a member of that or any other household 
unless he or she is--
            ``(1) a resident of the United States; and
            ``(2) either--
                    ``(A) a citizen or national of the United States;
                    ``(B) an alien lawfully admitted for permanent 
                residence as an immigrant as defined by sections 
                101(a)(15) and 101(a)(20) of the Immigration and 
                Nationality Act, excluding, among others, alien 
                visitors, tourists, diplomats, and students who enter 
                the United States temporarily with no intention of 
                abandoning their residence in a foreign country;
                    ``(C) an alien who has been granted the status of 
                Cuban and Haitian entrant, as defined in section 501(e) 
                of the Refugee Education Assistance Act of 1980 (Public 
                Law 96-422); or
                    ``(D) an individual who lawfully resides in the 
                United States in accordance with a Compact of Free 
                Association referred to in section 402(b)(2)(G) of the 
                Personal Responsibility and Work Opportunity 
                Reconciliation Act of 1996.
        The income (less, at State option, a pro rata share) and 
        financial resources of the individual rendered ineligible to 
        participate in the supplemental nutrition assistance program 
        under this subsection shall be considered in determining the 
        eligibility and the value of the allotment of the household of 
        which such individual is a member.''.
